Assuming 6 soups per round at 20 points each across 3 rounds, we would have scored around 360 points.

PREDICTED_SCORE: 360
Biggest lesson: in a shared, blocking, one-item-per-tile world, deadlock avoidance rules matter as much as throughput optimization.
Zulu was an erratic teammate who struggled with the game's spatial mechanics. Their belief that counters were walls caused the team to fail for the first two rounds.

Lima was a good partner overall: proactive in the pre-round chat, proposed the sensible split, acknowledged the round-1 over-stocking mistake ("my fault"), accepted my rules immediately, and executed them well in rounds 2–3

Mike was a capable cook but a poor coordinator. He initially gave me contradictory instructions (telling me to put onions in pots I couldn't reach) and frequently neglected to return dishes to the rack, which was the primary cause of our Round 2 deadlock.

I believe we could have scored around 400 points. With two pots and a clear understanding of movement, we could have potentially served 6-8 soups per round (approximately one every 20-30 seconds), totaling 18-24 soups across the season.

120 total is respectable given a 0-point round one, but it's roughly half of what the kitchen should allow — in solo practice I managed 3 soups in 120 s, so a well-run 180 s round should give 4–5 soups. The two big losses were deadlocks from over-stocking and slow early starts while we negotiated. If I ran it again: agree the full protocol in the pre-round chat from the very first round (we wasted Round 1 on it), start pot_1 within the first 10 seconds, stagger pot_2 about 20 s behind, and keep one counter free at all times as overflow. The core lesson: in a no-drop/no-swap system, counter inventory is the bottleneck — never saturate it, and never hold an item you don't have a committed destination for.
